transcript:
>> This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
Two U.S. Senate races are still too close to call.
In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola is leading Republican Senator Dan Sullivan
by about 600 votes.
In Mississippi, at last check, Democrat Scott Colon leads Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith
by fewer than 2000 votes.
Elise Catrine-Greg from Mississippi Public Broadcasting and the Gulf Newsroom reports.
>> Both candidates say they have lawyers monitoring the ballot count
and ready for legal challenges that will likely follow this race.
Here's Mississippi GOP Chair Mike Hurst.
>> Every outstanding ballot, every county, every deadline,
every legal option, we'll get our full attention.
We will not sleep until we know that our elections are secure.
>> Lee Parrott, a Cologne supporter, says she's cautiously optimistic about Cologne winning
because of changes to Mississippi's voter roll review system.
>> I think a lot of names were purged and the system that they used to purge was questionable.
>> Results likely won't be ready until at least Tuesday, the deadline for mail-in ballots.
For NPR News, I'm Elise Catrine-Greg in Jackson.
>> Democrats say they're planning to focus on lowering costs
and rooting out corruption when they take control of the House and Senate in January.
NPR's Sam Greenglass reports on what Democrats could get done
with President Trump still in the White House.
>> Democrats say first on their legislative agenda is restoring enhanced health subsidies
and reversing Medicaid cuts, reasserting authority over tariffs and trying to end the Iran war.
On these priorities, Democrats are aligned, but they'll need help from some Republicans
in the Senate and cooperation from President Trump.
Beyond this early agenda, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who's likely the next speaker
of the House, is promising bold, dramatic change, though what that looks like is not
totally clear.
Some newly elected moderate Democrats are wary of over-promising and under-delivering, while
a new crop of progressives warn against just tinkering around the edges.
100-plus new members will begin arriving in DC for orientation this weekend.
Sam Greenglass, NPR News, Washington.
>> U.S. employers ended 165,000 jobs in October, that's more than forecasters had expected.
Mark Zandi, the chief economist at Moody's Analytics, says the headline numbers tell
only part of the story.
>> Unemployment's down.
4.1% is, I'll take it, I mean, that's pretty close to what you consider full employment.
There's a lot of blemishes, though.
I mean, hiring remains very morbid, particularly for young people, and wage growth, that's
kind of key metric for most, to people with jobs, they want to make sure that their wages
are rising at a pace that's faster than inflation, and that's not happening.
>> Healthcare and transportation added jobs last month, while restaurants and construction
companies cut them.
This is NPR News in Washington.
The FBI has arrested the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex.
Federal prosecutors in Florida have charged Thomas Markle with one count of possessing
child sexual abuse material.
Authorities say it includes photos of Markle with underage girls.
The 82-year-old has denied the allegations.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services is restarting the certification of 19,000
new health insurance brokers, Alex Olgin reports.
>> In September, CMS unexpectedly froze all new broker licenses and ended 760,000 people's
health plans.
The agency claimed this was to fight fraudulent enrollments, which have landed a few brokers
in prison.
The moratorium caused chaos for brokers prepping for the November open enrollment period.
Johnny Wallin with Health Insurance Exchange Group is trying to rehire people.
>> I immediately started calling and messaging some of the people that we had that we ended
up having to let go because they're not being able to pay the license to help.
Democratic senators are now probing insurers.
They say plan cancellations are only possible because insurers were quietly colluding with
the Trump administration.
For NPR News, I'm Alex Olgin.
>> Tesla says it will wind down production of its Cybertruck in Texas next year.
The company says it will free up factory space to build more of Tesla's cyber-cab robo-taxis.
Sales have struggled since the Cybertruck went on sale in 2023.
I'm Windsor Johnston and PR News in Washington.

topics.text: Alaska Senate race: Democrat Mary Peltola leads Republican Dan Sullivan by about 600 votes
Mississippi Senate race: Democrat Scott Colon leads Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith by under 2,000 votes
Mississippi parties prepare lawyers for likely legal challenges as mail-in ballot deadline nears
Democrats outline early agenda for January: health subsidies, Medicaid cuts, tariffs, and Iran war
U.S. employers add 165,000 jobs in October, beating forecasts; young hiring and wages lag
FBI arrests Thomas Markle, father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, on child sexual abuse material charge
CMS resumes certifying 19,000 health insurance brokers after freezing new licenses in September
Democratic senators probe insurers over plan cancellations allegedly coordinated with Trump administration
Tesla to end Cybertruck production in Texas next year to free factory space for robotaxis
